title: Cache thrash & edge prompt degeneration: quantization experiment notes
content:
Summary:

Short version: during a mixed-length, bursty workload (short prefix prompts followed by long continuations), we observed reproducible degeneration (token repetition and semantic collapse) only when using AWQ-int8 kernels and only on sequences where the KV cache experienced transient eviction/compaction events. GPTQ-int8 and fp8 kernels did not show the same pattern. Profiling indicates rounding/noise accumulation in quantized attention key/value writes combined with a cache compaction path that temporarily rewrites cached entries.

Why this matters: these are realistic production patterns (chat systems that start short, then expand to long context). Degeneration at the model output level under quantized kernels can be subtle and only appears under cache churn; it bypasses our per-token perplexity monitors because overall token-level metrics look ok until the collapse starts.

Experiment setup (replicable details):
- Models: llama-2-13b-chat-like checkpoint (server conversion + same tokenization).
- Quant methods: AWQ (8-bit asymmetric weight quant, packing kernel v2), GPTQ (8-bit calibrated, packing kernel v1), FP8 baseline (emulated on float kernels).
- Kernels: custom awq_pack_v2, gptq_pack_v1, float_matmul_v1.
- Hardware: 4xA100-sxm-80GB (serving nodes), test client on separate node.
- Runtime: release branch runtime@v0.34 with dynamic KV-cache compaction enabled (threshold=0.7).
- Workload: synthetic chat workload with 60k requests over 2 hours, mix = {short_prompt (1-8 tokens): 65%, mid (20-80): 25%, long (512-2048): 10%}. Long requests are often follow-ups that append to existing session KV caches.
- Batch shape: dynamic, up to 64 tokens per request, batching window=8ms.
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency, per-token perplexity, repetition score (n-gram repeat rate), token-level KL divergence to FP8 baseline, KV cache size and compaction events timeline, memory allocation logs, CPU timelines for kernel selection.

Observations and data snippets:
- Repro rate: ~14% of long continuations under AWQ triggered a degeneration collapse (defined as >6 consecutive repeated tokens or drop in semantic coherence measured by BLEU-to-reference < 0.2). GPTQ-int8: ~1.3% (mostly noise), FP8: 0%.
- Latency/p99: AWQ shows marginally better p50 (x1.06 faster) but p99 increased by ~12% during the collapse windows (due to re-tries/fallbacks and extra cache compactions).
- KV compaction correlation: in 86% of collapse cases, a compaction event (cache entries moved/rewritten) occurs within the previous 2 tokens generated.

Example trace (abridged):
- request id: 0x7f9b1c
- prefix: "Summarize the following document: ..." (6 tokens)
- model begins generation -> kernel: awq_pack_v2 attention_matmul
- token N: compaction triggered (runtime log: "kv_compact start, retained 0.72")
- token N+1..N+5: repeated tokens "the the the the the" observed
- runtime debug: attention writebacks observed on GPU memory region 0x3bfa, write size matches packed-quant stride, small nonzero corrections applied in gather path

Profiling notes (what we captured):
- nvprof / CUPTI capture around compaction shows additional memcpy and small element-wise correction kernel executed immediately after compaction when AWQ kernel is used. These corrections are absent for GPTQ and FP kernels.
- Wall-clock ordering: quant-packing kernel writes compressed keys/values -> compaction path reads packed data, decompresses to temporary buffer, applies an "alignment correction" loop (single-threaded CUDA kernel in our stack), writes back to cache region. That correction loop has probabilistic rounding that in aggregate produces tiny biases in attention vectors.
- Attention heatmaps around collapse show a dramatic increase in self-attention mass on the last generated token (feedback loop). Hypothesis: tiny rounding shifts in keys push attention to favor recent tokens, which then get amplified by autoregression.

Micro-benchmarks (single-run):
- AWQ: key_write latency per-element: 0.21us (base), compaction + correction cost: +0.09us/element; correction introduces non-deterministic float differences (1e-3 to 1e-2 relative) vs unpacked float baseline.
- GPTQ: key_write 0.25us, compaction path uses quant-decode with vectorized kernel -> no single-thread correction, relative diffs <1e-4.

Hypotheses and root causes (working):
1) AWQ packing v2 uses a compact + correction strategy to reduce quantization bias for average-case workloads. That correction is not numerically stable when interleaved with KV compaction that rearranges temporal order (so rounding distribution changes at runtime).
2) Cache compaction triggers decompress/encode paths that are not numerically equivalent to the original incremental write path (ordering + accumulation differences).
3) The combination of (1) and (2) pushes a small attention shift which is amplified by autoregressive decoding leading to repetition.

Quick experiments run to validate hypotheses:
- Disabled correction loop in AWQ pack (dev flag): collapse rate dropped to 2.5% but raw generation quality decreased slightly on edge-cases (more hallucinations).
- Forced deterministic packed-order merging (serialize compaction with token generation): collapse rate dropped to 0.8% but p50 latency increased by 9%.
- Increase compaction threshold (avoid compaction until 0.85 occupancy): collapse rate down to 3.1%, resource usage up ~6%.

Implications for production:
- AWQ kernels in current packing+correction implementation produce best throughput in steady-state but have a non-negligible risk for rare but high-impact degeneration events when combined with dynamic cache compaction.
- The SLA tradeoff is between small steady-state gains vs. occasional output-quality regressions. For chat products where coherence is critical, that tradeoff is unacceptable without mitigation.

Actionable next steps (short-term):
1) Disable the AWQ correction kernel behind a feature flag for Dedicated clusters serving chat workloads with aggressive compaction. Roll out to canary 10% traffic. (owner: Diego)
2) Implement an alternative vectorized correction kernel to replace the single-threaded loop (bench target: performance parity with current pack + accuracy parity with disabled-correction). (owner: Priya)
3) Add an anomaly monitor: detect sharp increase in 3-gram repetition over 10k tokens and trigger automatic fallback to GPTQ or FP kernels for that session. (owner: SRE: Samir)
4) Add an A/B test in console to measure user-visible impact (engage product to craft metric: "session-quality-drop" events).

Longer-term investigations:
- Formal numerical analysis of pack+correction under reorderings (work with applied-ml team to quantify worst-case accumulative bias).
- Revisit compaction algorithm to ensure stable ordering or use commutative reduction primitives to avoid ordering-dependent bias.
- Explore hybrid fallback: keep AWQ for new tokens but re-evaluate attention distributions periodically under FP8 for sessions crossing long-context thresholds.

Open questions / discussion points:
- Is it acceptable to trade p50 improvements for rare but severe quality drops? Which SLAs should force fallback?
- Is the cost of vectorized correction worth the engineering effort vs raising compaction thresholds?
- Do we need to treat KV-compaction as a first-class operation in quantized kernels (i.e., provide atomic in-kernel compaction routines)?

Appendix (debug snippets):
- Runtime log grep: "kv_compact start" shows an average of 32 compactions/hour per node under our workload; during peaks this spikes to ~120/h.
- Command used for workload repro:
  ./benchmark_client --model llm-13b --quant awq --clients 128 --dur 7200 --mix-file mixes/mar-chat-bursty.json --enable-kv-compaction

Notes to reviewers: this doc is an intermediate dump from the investigation. I intentionally included raw traces and hypotheses — please annotate if you've run similar reproductions or if you have ideas for kernel-level mitigation.

Maya
